PORT COLBORNE ELEVATORS On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, in view of the limited capacity of the government elevators at Port Colborne, the serious grain congestion which is occurring and the consequent diversion of the grain to Buffalo, I would ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) whether the government contemplates the enlargement of the elevators at Port Colborne. The capacity of these elevators is only 2,000,000 bushels, and a great number of vessels are tied up there and other vessels are being diverted to the port of Buffalo.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): As hon. members know, that port is used as a transfer point in order to transfer cargoes from the large lake vessels to the smaller St. Lawrence river boats. The problem to be solved is the shortage of the small boats in relation to the number of the large boats arriving at the elevator. Subject to further study, I would say that an increase in the storage facilities would not be a solution of the problem. Last year, and for several years past, the elevator has handled more grain than any other elevator in Canada, handling over 70,000,000 bushels of grain last year. I shall be glad to ask my departmental officers to give attention to the point raised by the hon. member, and if there is anything that can be done I can assure him that the government will give it favourable consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I am within the judgment of the house when I say that I rarely refer to newspaper criticism of my-
self. I realize that one of the incidents of the position which I occupy is that I must be criticized. The other evening I had occasion to direct attention to an editorial which appeared in Le Droit, and it has been alleged that I did not correctly interpret or translate the sense of that editorial. The editorial appeared in the issue of April 20, and I am sure that hon. members will realize that I am conscious of my imperfections in pronunciation when I do not endeavour to read it in the original. I have asked the Clerk of the House if it would be possible to provide me with a translation made by an official translator, and in order that there may be no misapprehension as to what this article contains, I wild read the translation I have received. It is as follows:
These Accusations
Attack on the Postmaster General-Political
favouritism-The rights of the Ministers [DOT]-Fanaticism and Bilingualism
The Postmaster General, Mr. Veniot, has been this week and will continue to be for several days more, the object of the attacks of the Conservative opposition, so long as the house has not passed the estimates of his department.
These attacks hardly surprise us, since Mr. Veniot himself has done all he could to provoke them. It is a crime for certain people to see that the constitution is respected, to see that the two official languages are on a footing of equality and that the field of action of the French language is enlarged a little. We do not fear to say that certain people object to the father of the bilingual postage stamp more than to the minister who is charged with favouritism.
And these charges of favouritism, what do they amount to? We are not silly enough to ignore that notwithstanding the existence of the Civil Service Commission, political colour has something to do in the choice and appointment of a candidate, to whatever position he may aspire. Political patronage is still being exercised. The government endeavours to appoint as many of its own supporters as it can, and this is quite human. Should it be asked, perchance, to practise self-abnegation to the extent of giving the preference to its opponents? No, and this is why it may be said without danger of error, that under the present administration a Liberal has a better chance of entering the civil service than a Conservative. And should Mr. Bennett become Prime Minister to-morrow, it is quite probable that the Conservatives would have easier access to public office. And so, Mr. Veniot stands at good advantage in the present debate. All he has to do to defend his ease, is to admit himself guilty of all the charges laid against him, while stating vigorously that his political opponents did much worse when they were in office.
But the minister has no need of using this argument ad hominem. He has already given the number of postmasters dismissed under his administration and stated in each ease, the reason for such dismissal.
It is also alleged as a crime against Mr. Veniot that he has not always accepted the

Privilege-Mr. Bennett
candidates recommended by the Civil Service Commission, and the case of Mr. Whittaker is mentioned with the contention that the minister did not want this man as postmaster at Simeoe. The commission itself had declared this returned soldier unable to fill the job and Mr. Veniot had another returned man appointed in his place.
According to the Civil Service Act, the ministers have the right to reject the candidates of the commission. And this is practised in every department. Thus, during the last three years, sixty-one candidates were rejected in this way: four in the Department of Agriculture, five in the Department of Finance, nine in the Department of National Revenue, twenty-three in the Post Office Department, five in the Department of Public Works, one in the Department of Justice, etc. If one takes into consideration the fact that the Post Office Department employs nearly eleven thousand hands, it is evident that Mr. Veniot has not taken advantage of this privilege any more than his colleagues, but even less, due allowance being made for the number of employees.
And so, there is no reason to feel uneasy with regard to Mr. Veniot. The administration of his department is as good as in the past if not better, and the postal service has not retrograded as far as we know. All this noise around certain appointments or dismissals is like a tempest in a tea-pot: it is the madness of fanaticism against a minister who is convinced that the sun shines for everybody and acts accordingly. A minister who, like Mr. Veniot, tries to put in practice the letter as well as the spirit of the constitution, deserves the support of all political and national elements.
That is the article which I shall now place on Hansard with the original. The following is the original:
Ces accusations
Une offensive eontre le ministre des Postes.- Favoritisme politique.-Les droits des mi-nistres.-Fanatisme et bilinguisme.
M. Veniot, ministre des Postes, a ete cette semaine le point de mire des attaques de l'op-position conservatrice, et il le sera encore pendant plusieurs jours, tant que les credits de son ministere n'auront pas ete votes.
Ces attaques ne nous etonnent guere, puisque M. Veniot lui-meme a tout fait pour les provo-quer. C'est un crime, pour certaines gens, que de faire respecter la Constitution, que de placer reellement les deux langues officielles sur un pied d'egalite, que d'elargir un peu le champ de rayonnement de la langue fransaise. Nous ne craignons pas d'affirmer que l'on en veut plus au pere du timbre bilingue qu'au ministre soup-?onne de favoritisme.
Que valent d'ailleurs ces accusations de favoritisme? Nous ne sommes pas assez nai'fs pour ignore!' que, malgre l'existence de la commission du service civil, la couleur politique a quelque chose a faire dans le choix et la nomination d'un eandidat, a quelque poste qu'il aspire. Le patronage politique continue de s'exercer. Le gouvernement s'efforce de nommer le plus possible de ses partisans, et c'est tres humain. Fau-drait-il, par hasard, lui demander de pousser l'abnegation jusqu'a donner la preference a ses adversaires? Non, et e'est pourquoi on peut admettre, sans courir le risque de se tromper, que, sous l'administration actuelle, un liberal a
plus de chance d'entrer dans le service civil qu'un conservateur. Et si jamais M. Bennett etait demain premier ministre il est assez probable que les conservateurs auraient un acefes plus facile aux fonctions administratives. Aussi, M. Veniot a-t-il beau jeu dans la discussion actuelle. Pour les fins de son argumentation, il n'a qu'a se reconnaitre coupable de tout ce dont on l'accuse tout en criant bien fort que ses adversaires politiques avaient fait pire lorsqu'ils etaient au pouvoir.
Mais le ministre des Postes n'a pas besoin d'user de cet argument ad hominem. Il a deja fait connaitre le nombre des maitres de poste congedies sous son administration et donne, pour chaque cas, la raison du renvoi.
On fait egalement un crime a M. Veniot de ne pas avoir toujours accepte les candidats pre-sentes par la commission du service civil, et l'on cite le cas de M. Whittaker dont le ministre n'aurait pas voulu comme maitre de poste de Simeoe. Ce veteran avait ete reconnu par la commission elle-meme incapable de remplir ses fonctions et M. Veniot fit nommer a sa place un autre veteran.
D'apres la loi du service civil, les ministres ont le droit de rejeter les candidats de la commission. Et cela se pratique dans tous les mi-nisteres. Ainsi au cours des trois clernieres an-nees, il y a eu soixante et un ref us de la sorte: 4 au ministere de l'Agriculture, 5 aux Finances, 9 au Revenu national, 23 aux Postes, 5 aux Travaux publics, un au ministere de la Justice, etc. Si l'on tient compte du fait qu'il y a au ministere des Postes pres de onze mille employes, il faut en venir a la conclusion que M. Veniot n'a pas use de ce privilege plus que ses collegues et meme que, toutes proportions gar-dees, il en a use moins.
Il n'y a done pas lieu de s'alarmer sur le compte de M. Veniot. Son ministere est aussi bien administre que par le pass6, sinon mieux, et le service des postes n'a pas, que l'on saehe, retrograde. Tout ce tapage autour de certaines nominations ou demissions, e'est une tem-pete dans un verre d'eau, c'est la rage du fanatisme eontre un ministre qui est convaincu que le soleil brille pour tout le monde et qui agit en consequence. Parliamentary News
An unjust attack. The Conservative opposition
keeps up its obstruction of the Postmaster General's estimates (By Charles Michaud)
The leader of the opposition stated yesterday that "'Le Droit" had accused the Conservatives of making war on the Postmaster General because the latter is an Acadian and consequently of French descent. "Le Droit" has never said anything of the kind. The question is who could have so misinformed Mr. Bennett. Accordingly, the editor in chief of this newspaper immediately wrote, this morning, the following letter to the leader of the opposition :
Hon. R. B. Bennett,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I see by this morning's newspapers that you have accused "Le Droit" of having insinuated that the Conservative opposition bore ill-will to Mr. Veniot on account of his Acadian parentage. In view of the violence with which you have attacked "Le Droit" in this matter, I would ask you to read this letter at the next sitting of the House of Comons.
Believe me, etc.
Let us not forget that this Mr. Bennett who unjustly attacks "Le Droit" is the same Mr. Bennett who, Thursday last, in the House of Commons, awarded the following certificate to Mr. Edwards, who had just been called away by death:
"No man could point to a single observation that he had ever made in which he attacked any man's religion or denied to anyone of his fellow-citizens the right to worship his own God under his own vine and fig-tree. He had that tolerance which sometimes was denied to him."
The Grand Master of the Orange Order of Ontario, author of "The Wedge", a book which bears on its cover the picture of a priest, armed with an axe, destroying British institutions, must have smiled in his grave on hearing such praise. We, who know better, find the author of the lines just above quoted rather ill-acquainted with the deeds of the deceased member of parliament.
I did not deal with this matter yesterday because I was in the chamber but a very

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put, I desire to make one or two observations. I was not present during the discussion yesterday in connection with the Post Office estimates; but I have been visited by a gentleman whom I regard as being a highly reliable person and I ascertained from him that in the city of St. John a situation exists of the gravest character. I have consulted with members who represent that constituency in the house, and I have been advised that rumours are very prevalent in the streets of that city and elsewhere in New Brunswick about that situation. I refer to the situation in connection with the district office, that is, the office responsible for the conduct of the postal business in that, province. I observe, from looking at the debate, that reference was made to three gentlemen: Mr. Woods, who is the chief; Mr. Emerson, and Mr. Griffiths. It is apparently a common rumour on the streets of St. John that the junior inspector had very grossly insulted his senior officer; that everyone knows of the matter; that officers have been sent from Ottawa to take charge of the office; that grave irregularities have been discovered; that reports have been made to the Postmaster General or his deputy-my informant is not
quite certain as to which-and they disclosed a situation that is very serious from the public standpoint.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) who is temporarily leading the house, that if will serve no useful purpose to precipitate further discussion upon the Post Office estimates, thereby tvasting public time, until we have before us the files connected with the matters to [DOT]which I have referred. The gentleman to whom I referred at the outset came to me saying he felt it was my duty to bring these matters to the attention of the house, and I would be derelict in my duty did I not stand in my place and state the position which I now take. It is my desire and the desire of those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, not to impede public business, not to take up time for the sake of doing so, and I suggest that if the minister would provide that the files dealing with this situation be made available, possibly in one of the rooms of the house, with one of the members of his staff present, it might enable us to ascertain to what extent these reports are justified; for according to the information which I have received, Mr. Speaker, in the manner I have indicated, the minister has received very definite information touching the conduct of at least one of the inspectors involving very serious allegations regarding honesty and the dealing with and payment of moneys. All these are matters which we should not permit longer to continue to float as rumours vague and undefined about the streets of a great city, but rather we should get to the bottom of the matter, and if there is anything in it, we should deal with it at once. If there is nothing in it, that is the end of it, and the rumours are disposed of.
I gave my promise that I would endeavour to have this matter brought up at the earliest possible moment, and in the very earnest desire to expedite rather than impede the transaction of public business, I make the suggestion that the post office estimates be held over until such time as we shall have had an opportunity to investigate the matters to which I have referred, and then having obtained the information, instead of wasting the time of the house trying to get the information piecemeal here, we should be able to precipitate a discussion around the concrete matter to which I have referred. In that event there would be no delay, no waste of time, and no opportunity for its being said that we had in any sense delayed rather than assisted in the conduct of public business. When I say "we", I mean any of the members of the house who seek information in this way; because I realize, as you must realize, Mr. St. John Post Office

Speaker, having occupied the office of postmaster general, how impossible it is for a minister to get copies of all the files prepared at one time. But we might be able to deal with the situation as I have indicated, and in that way precipitate a discussion that would be concrete and directly connected with the matters we have been discussing.
There are a number of files that have been mentioned that we might thus be able to deal with; I do not recall what they were, but they were mentioned yesterday. As the Minister of Finance has stated that it is proposed to deal with the estimates of the Public Works department for the moment, we can deal with them in committee, and if there is any other business we might dispose of that to-day, and then to-morrow morning we ask that the opportunity be afforded to the members on this side of the house, with the minister's official present, to inspect the files to which I have referred to see whether or not these reports are warranted and what they disclose in connection with the post office situation in the district of New Brunswick, the headquarters being the city of St. John.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the observations made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) are not at all unreasonable; indeed, on 'behalf of the government I desire to say that they are most reasonable, and I speak as one who has been in apposition. I am sure that my colleague the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) will be prepared to view the suggestion made by the hon. leader of the opposition in the spirit in which it is offered, and to regard the request that he made on behalf of the opposition as a most reasonable one. I will leave my hon. friend the Postmaster General to deal with that.
It is the intention of the government today to go into supply on Public Works, and if we make sufficient progress there are some bills on the order paper standing in the name of .the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) that we might advance.

I would like to say a word before we go into supply. I feel that the request of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is a very reasonable one. So much did I feel that such a request, if made, would be a reasonable one, that when the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) yesterday asked me about that matter, after I had attempted in some way to explain the situation although without going fully into it, and he interjected the question whether I

would lay the correspondence on the table, I immediately said yes; but after due consideration, and in view of the fact that the investigation into some of these difficulties is now going on, I was going to suggest to the hon. member for York-Sunbury to-day, if I went into supply, that the correspondence be not laid on the table, but that he have an opportunity with me or with one of my officials to go fully into the correspondence, because I felt that while we were carrying on this investigation and endeavouring to discover the foundation of the difficulties in the St. John district it might not be right to lay all this information on the table. I am therefore pleased indeed to accept the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition that the original file in the possession of an official of the department be placed in the hands, say, of the hon. member for York-Sunbury and whomever he wishes to have associated with him, so that he can go over the whole thing.
Let me say, to correct what is perhaps a wrong impression that grave irregularities were discovered at the time the two gentlemen mentioned yesterday had visited the post office at St. John-

I desire to assure my
hon. friend the Postmaster General that I was simply trying to indicate to him the information that had been conveyed to me, and I thought it was in the public interest that the matter should be cleared up. I was not indicating whether I believed it or did not believe it, but merely stating that such rumors were prevalent.

It is not quite consistent
with what really took place. What took place was this: There were charges made of irregularities, and charges of want of discipline. There was the report of this fight, if I may use the word, between the chief of the district, Mr. Woods, and one of the subordinate officers.
Which one was that?

Mr. Griffiths. When I
heard of this, and knowing, previous to that, that there was some lack of discipline in that office, I sent to St. John two men who we consider are experts, one in operation and the other in financial administration, not at that time to go into any charges made, but to start an investigation into the disciplinary end and discuss with these two fighting fellows, if I may use the term, the cause of

St. John Post Office
this lack of discipline and lack of respect on the part of an inspector for his superior officer, the superintendent. They went into that, and they brought back to the office here in Ottawa statements of charges touching financial affairs. Those are on file, and that part of the investigation is to be continued.
I shall be only too pleased to submit these papers.

Perhaps I might ask my hon. friend a further question, with his permission. My informant had been advised that these two gentlemen-one of them, I think, was Fortier and the other Underwood -had gone down there and that the minister himself had visited St. John during the Easter recess and was thoroughly familiar with the situation that developed. That was the information given to me, and it might enable the minister to make a statement in regard to it.

I was in St. John at the
opening of the airport there-no, it was the Easter recess; my hon. friend is right. I think these two men were there before I got there. I knew they had been in St. John, but I did not know they were there at the time. I visited St. John for two days and I found these gentlemen there. They had been there two days. I met them in the hotel. I knew what they were there for, because instructions had been issued from Ottawa. They remained another day, and then came back to Ottawa. They made me familiar with the disciplinary end of this fracas between the officials, but I told them I did not want to hear further about any irregularities until I got back to the office.

The offer made by the Postmaster General is very satisfactory so far as it goes, but it does seem to me to be a little narrow. He said we are to have an opportunity of examining the original file, but I failed to hear him say that we would have the privilege of making copies of any of the documents we might require. I should like to have that incorporated in the offer.
I may say to the hon. gentleman that in view of what took place yesterday I have had copies of the file made, so there will be no difficulty in that regard.
Since the house appears to be in a very friendly mood at the moment, and as the minister is apparently dealing courteously with members on this side of the house-
He always does.

There have been occasions when that has been in question, and such occasions may again arise.
I wish to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that although the matter of increase in salaries of our postal workers has been raised, and although he has protested again and again that he made recommendations to the Civil Service Commission in this regard, no statement as to the character of those recommendations has yet been laid on the table of the house, and I would ask him to be prepared to table a copy of any recommendations made by him to the Civil Service Commission in relation to postal salaries.

I laid those on the table
over a week ago, and I referred to them yesterday. They are in the possession of the house.
I refer to the minister's personal recommendations to the commission.
Yes.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is rather interesting to hear my hon. friend repeat the question which for two years I have endeavoured to answer to the effect that the policy of the government was as far as possible to erect public buildings only in places where the service was such that they were urgently required. It is rather interesting also to note- and I may say to my hon. friends on this side of the house that I rather hesitate to refer to this fact-that of the vote for public buildings in the province of Nova Scotia amounting to $185,300, the expeditures in constituencies represented by government members of the house total only $30,000, if the glance I have taken over them is correct.

And none at all in the
other constituencies represented by Conservatives.

Of the total vote, $155,000 is to be expended in constituencies represented by gentlemen on the other side of the house. The total expenditures in constituencies rep-

resented by gentlemen on this side are the two items of $15,000 each for the erection of post office buildings which are urgently required. The $15,000 for Hantsport is a start, the total for building, fittings, grading, sidewalks and contingencies being placed at $24,500. The $15,000 for Sherbrooke is to provide a site and commence a building, the total cost of which will be $28,500. So that the total expenditures contemplated by these two items are just in the vicinity of $50,000.

What is the total cost
of the Hantsport building?

For building, fittings, sidewalks, clerk of works and contingencies, $24,500. I should hardly expect my hon. friend to think that we could spend $185,300 in the province without spending something in some Liberal constituency.

I should be astonished if
it were otherwise, knowing the minister as well as I do and the operations of his mind. But let us outline the situation as he has given it. He says that the buildings are to be placed only where urgently required. He goes on to tell us that out of that $185,000 all but $30,000 is to be spent in constituencies represented by Conservative members. Let us take the very first item, $25,000, for the Halifax immigration building. That is merely a bookkeeping entry, representing an amount paid by one department of government to another; it is paid by the Public Works department to the Department of Railways and Canals, and no money at all will be passed, although they may go through the form of issuing a cheque. So that as regards that item at all events the minister's assertion is not carried out. You are renting accommodation from another department of government; that is all that means. And with respect to every other item in the total for Nova Scotia, of $185,300, they are all simply repairs or additions to existing buildings. But that is not what I asked the minister about at all. What I asked him was to give us a statement as to the policy of the government with respect to the erection of public buildings, now that .that policy has been resumed since the war. He has told us that buildings are to be erected where they are urgently required. May I ask him whether there are any other points in Nova Scotia, outside Hantsport and Sherbrooke, where public buildings are urgently required. An analysis of the vote does not bear out the situation as he has described it to the house.

I know my hon. friend
wants to be fair, and I take it-if I may put

Supply-Public Works-Nova Scotia
it this way without seeming to be impolite- that he has read over the facts in regard to which he speaks. He need only go to the third item, with reference to the establishment of new buildings, Halifax naval and ordnance, to realize that we are spending there, not for repairs as he has stated, but in the erection of a new building in that riding, which I am sure he will not argue is represented by any of the Liberal members, the sum of $50,000. That quite contradicts the statement he has made. As I say, I know he made it unintentionally and in good faith; but it proves that he has suspicions which are absolutely unfounded. That is the situation in that one riding alone, and I doubt very much whether the new construction there is more urgently required than new buildings in any other place. But we are spending there, as I have stated, $50,000.

Have tenders been called
for in connection with these buildings? I admit at once that I overlooked the new ordnance building.
I know it was unintentional.

I did not wish to be unfair to the minister. But I would point out that this $50,000 is purely a departmental matter; it is not for a building to be put up in the interests of the general public. It will never be a public utility such as the building at Hantsport or Sherbrooke. It has no doubt been asked for by the technical officers of the Department of National Defence, and so far as the public are concerned they will never be allowed inside it. Will these buildings be put up by tender and, if so, will Mr. A. S. MacMillan be the successful tenderer?

Mr. MacMillan may
construct these buildings if he is the lowest tenderer.

I presume your department
will see that he is the lowest tenderer, because he seems to get all contracts let by the department in Nova Scotia.

My hon. friend does not

And I can satisfy him by going over the tenders in connection with various works in this country, from one coast to the other, that a great proportion of those who are the lowest tenderers are not supporters of this government.

Not in our province.

I do not believe that either my hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman will get up and say that the men who have tendered for public works in Canada, whether it be buildings or harbours or anything else, have not been judged on the sole question as to whether or not their tenders were the lowest. What is the population of Hantsport, what is the public revenue, and what departments of government are intended to be housed in the building here? The same with reference to Sherbrooke.

The proposed building at
Hantsport will be a one and a half storey brick structure and will provide accommodation for the post office, with living quarters for the caretaker. The post office is at present located in a section of the ground floor of a large building. In regard to the other one-
What is the revenue?

I want to call attention to this, because it will appeal to my hon. friend that this site is a place where a public building is really needed. An order in council was passed on January 7, 1914. Bear in mind the date-January 7, 1914. My hon. friend will be one of the last to argue that sites were selected in 1914 for public buildings which were not required for the public service; he will remember that those sites were selected by his friends. This site was purchased in 1914, and I think perhaps that will allay the suspicion he seems to have that this is not necessary

I have not said anything of the kind; I do not intend to oppose the vote but I ana asking the government for a declaration of policy which will cover the whole Dominion. I am not opposing this vote but it is up to the minister to justify and explain it.

As I told my hon. friend, the total is expected to be about $24,500. The 3ite has been already provided.

Yes, but we are getting along, making some progress; we cannot do it all in a year.
What will be the total cost of the Sherbrooke building
I gave it before, but I shall be glad to repeat it. It is expected that the total cost, including the site, which has not been provided, will be $28,500, of which $1,500 is set apart for the site.

Very much the same as the other town; about 700.
Is the minister sure of that? My information is that it is very much less.
My information is that according to the census of 1921 the population was 679, and it is greater at present.

The revenue was $3,291.

I do not wish to oppose either of these votes; in fact I am very much in favour of them. I am glad the minister has listened to the advice of the members for those districts and given post offices to these towns, because I believe these smaller

places are entitled to public buildings. However, I must direct his attention to the fact that he has not provided one building in any constituency with the exception of these two which are represented by friends of the government.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says hear, hear. He is living in the dark ages, when the spoils system was in effect. If that is the policy in the province of Quebec I want to tell my hon. friend that in Nova Scotia we are above that sort of thing. My hon. friend belongs to the last generation; the spoils system is out of date not only in this country but in ever3' civilized country throughout the world.
Why?

Because we should be treated equally. We are entitled to some consideration; we pay the same revenue.
Now I am going to turn my attention to the minister for a moment. I am glad to see that at last he has decided to make a start in these two towns. A few moments ago we were told that the site for the Hantsport building was purchased in 1914, so it is time the building was constructed. But I want to direct the minister's attention to another town nearly twice as large as this and with three times the revenue. I refer to the town of Bridgetown in Nova Scotia. In 1925, when this government was in power, the then Minister of Public Works visited Bridgetown and was so impressed with the need for a public building that he decided to purchase a site, for which $5,000 was paid.
